Heterogeneous catalysis OurBigBook.com
The University of Washington's Decomposition of H₂O₂ with MnO₂ describes a supervised demonstration using solid manganese dioxide and hydrogen peroxide listed as 30%. Its cylinder version uses a spatula to introduce the solid; the stated readout is immediate molecular oxygen bubbles and heat production. An alternate bottle version replaces the contents of a tea bag with the solid and suspends it above the liquid. Releasing the bag brings it into contact with the liquid. The bag-above-liquid stage supplies a before-contact comparison; the page gives no timed gas collection, replicated blank trials or quantitative reaction rates.[ref]
The balanced net chemical equation is 2H2​O2​⟶2H2​O+O2​. Appearance of gas after contact supports a contact-dependent acceleration of decomposition under these conditions. It does not distinguish surface conversion from a contribution of dissolved material, establish regeneration, or measure an activation energy. The simultaneous heat release also means that temperature can change after contact. A matched no-solid comparison and an empty-bag comparison would test background decomposition and the bag's contribution; these are proposed controls, not reported trials. The catalysed peroxide comparison supplies a complementary inspected teaching experiment with separate single-addition and paired-addition comparisons.

Catalysed peroxide comparison

Words: 414
Heterogeneous catalysis OurBigBook.com
A simple motivating comparison is visible gas evolution from hydrogen peroxide, whose net chemical equation is
2H2​O2​⟶2H2​O+O2​.
(30)
The products are water and oxygen. The Royal Society of Chemistry's teaching resource uses small test tubes and droppers, hydrogen peroxide labelled 5–10 volumes, solutions of metal salts including copper(II) sulfate, and approximately 1molL−1 sodium hydroxide. Its qualitative procedure tests additions singly and in pairs to tubes containing about 1cm depth of hydrogen peroxide. It reports the expected classroom result that the additions individually are not effective under those conditions, whereas the solids produced by mixing metal-salt solution with sodium hydroxide give effective heterogeneous catalysis. This is the resource's expected observation, not a newly measured ranking.[ref]
A focused adaptation compares four matched tubes: no addition, copper(II) sulfate alone, sodium hydroxide alone, and the pair. Use equal initial hydrogen peroxide amounts, identical tubes and the same starting temperature. Record stock concentrations and added volumes; add water to the other tubes to match the total added liquid. Additions can first be checked without hydrogen peroxide to distinguish precipitation from gas evolution. Start a timer at contact, mix consistently, and observe gas evolution over the same interval. These matching controls are proposed improvements to the qualitative resource, not claimed details of its original trials. Follow its supervised chemical-handling requirements; the stated strengths describe its teaching protocol rather than an unrestricted recipe.
The immediate readout is relative bubbling, together with whether a solid appears. More vigorous bubbling in the paired tube supports faster conversion under the comparison conditions; it does not identify the solid's exact composition or establish a unique reaction mechanism. Bubble counts are not a calibrated reaction rate: bubble sizes, gas retention and warming can differ. For a quantitative extension, use a freely moving gas syringe to record collected volume V(t) and compare early slopes dV/dt at matched temperature and pressure; check for leaks and repeat runs. This extension is a measurement proposal, not source-reported gas traces.
The paired treatment also changes pH and produces a surface, so the four tubes alone cannot assign the whole effect to one microscopic catalytic step. A filtered-liquid comparison and a separated, washed-solid comparison would help distinguish dissolved and solid contributions, although washing itself can change the active material. More gas at one time establishes neither a changed equilibrium constant nor indefinite catalyst reuse. The open gas-evolution experiment is especially unsuitable as a demonstration that two closed mixtures reach the same chemical equilibrium: the escaping oxygen changes the constraints. The reversible model above supplies that separate explanation. No numerical experimental rate constants, barrier heights or gas volumes are asserted here.

Catalyst

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Catalysis OurBigBook.com
A catalyst makes a chemical reaction proceed faster by participating in an alternative reaction mechanism and being regenerated. This makes repeated conversion possible: the same catalyst can help many successive reactants become reaction products. An enzyme is a biological catalyst. The overall standard change in Gibbs free energy is unchanged; see the IUPAC Gold Book: catalyst.
Regeneration does not mean that the catalyst sits unchanged throughout every step. For example, a schematic reaction mechanism can temporarily bind A to a catalyst C in a reaction intermediate AC:
A+CACnet:A​⇌AC,⇌B+C,⇌B.​
(31)
Adding the steps cancels both the reaction intermediate AC and the catalyst C from the net chemical equation. AC is produced and later consumed; C is used and later recovered. These letters describe possible roles, not a measured reaction mechanism. The alternative route is useful only if its chemical kinetics permits faster conversion. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §12.7: catalysts and alternative mechanisms.
For a worked barrier example, consider an idealized reversible A-to-B conversion at fixed temperature T=300K. Stipulate standard molar Gibbs free energy levels GA∘​=0 and GB∘​=−20kJmol−1, with effective transition state levels 80 without a catalyst and 50kJmol−1 with a catalyst. Use the same standard states and the same zero for both routes; the catalytic route includes the regenerated C at both endpoints. Unlike the separate potential-energy profile example, this illustration uses Gibbs free energy at one specified temperature.
The Gibbs energy of activation is measured from the starting endpoint in the chosen direction. Thus the four barriers are
ΔGf,uncat‡∘​ΔGr,uncat‡∘​​=80−0=80,=80−(−20)=100,​ΔGf,cat‡∘​ΔGr,cat‡∘​​=50−0=50,=50−(−20)=70,​all in kJmol−1.
(32)
Both directional barriers fall by 30kJmol−1. The endpoint difference stays Δr​G∘=−20kJmol−1.
To turn those barriers into rate constants, use the Eyring form of transition state theory for this effective first-order reaction pair, with a common prefactor and unit probability of successful passage:
k=νexp(−RTΔG‡∘​),ν=hkB​T​.
(33)
Here kB​ is the Boltzmann constant, h is the Planck constant, and R is the molar gas constant. The common prefactor cancels from the comparisons. These Gibbs energies of activation are not the empirical activation energy Ea​ of the Arrhenius equation. With the stipulated value R=8.314462618Jmol−1K−1, the speedup is
kf,uncat​kf,cat​​=kr,uncat​kr,cat​​=exp(8.314462618×30030000​)≈1.67248×105.
(34)
The exponent is a dimensionless quantity: convert 30kJmol−1 to 30000Jmol−1 before dividing by RT. The exponential function explains why a modest barrier reduction can have a dramatic kinetic effect. This number follows from the chosen free-energy barriers and common prefactor; it is not a universal catalytic multiplier or a prediction across temperatures.
Assume ideal thermodynamic activities with a common concentration standard state, and directional rate laws Jf​=kf​[A] and Jr​=kr​[B]. At chemical equilibrium, equal reaction rates give K=[B]/[A]=kf​/kr​ for this model. The barriers give
Kuncat​=e−100000/(RT)e−80000/(RT)​=e20000/(RT)=e−70000/(RT)e−50000/(RT)​=Kcat​≈3035.58.
(35)
The catalyst speeds up both directions, so it changes how quickly chemical equilibrium is approached without changing this equilibrium constant. For a general chemical reaction, the thermodynamic relation is K=exp[−Δr​G∘/(RT)] with consistent standard states; an arbitrary multistep reaction mechanism need not permit K=kf​/kr​ for two measured rate constants. At the same temperature, pressure, and thermodynamic activities, a catalyst also leaves the actual overall reaction change in Gibbs free energy unchanged. See 13.3 Shifting Equilibria: Le Châtelier’s Principle (§13.3: a catalyst does not shift equilibrium). To drive an unfavourable overall conversion, a process such as energy coupling must change the combined transformation.

Precatalyst

Words: 26
Catalyst OurBigBook.com
A supplied precursor that must be chemically converted into the catalytically active form. Activation stoichiometry need not equal the reagent consumption of each subsequent catalytic turnover.

Transition state theory (k=(kB​T/h)exp[−ΔG‡∘/(RT)])

Words: 367 Articles: 8
Catalyst OurBigBook.com
Transition state theory relates an elementary reaction's rate constant to a Gibbs energy of activation. The Eyring expression used in the catalyst example assumes every passage counted at the transition state succeeds. More generally, a factor accounting for unsuccessful passage multiplies it. Comparing barriers alone gives the quoted speedup only when the remaining prefactors agree. Free-energy profiles can depend on temperature, so the example's values at 300K do not determine a temperature curve. See the IUPAC Gold Book: transition state theory.
Force-tilted activation barrier (k(F)=k0​eFΔx/(kB​T))
Words: 81
Transition state theory OurBigBook.com
A constant tensile force changes a one-coordinate free-energy landscape from G0​(x) to G0​(x)−Fx. To first order, an escape barrier decreases by FΔx, where Δx is the saddle-to-initial-minimum displacement at zero force. An approximately fixed attempt prefactor gives the displayed rate law. Its characteristic force is F0​=kB​T/Δx. Large changes in saddle location or competing pathways invalidate a constant activation distance. The barrier is measured relative to the initial state; an absolute saddle energy is not enough to determine an escape rate.
Activation volume (ΔV‡∘)
Words: 45
Transition state theory OurBigBook.com
The pressure derivative of the standard Gibbs energy of activation: ΔV‡∘=(∂ΔG‡∘/∂p)T​. In the corresponding rate convention, ΔV‡∘=−RT(∂lnk/∂p)T​. A negative value makes increasing pressure accelerate the reaction. Solvent reorganization can contribute as well as the intrinsic reacting geometry.
Activation entropy (ΔS‡∘)
Words: 30
Transition state theory OurBigBook.com
The standard entropy difference between the activated-complex reference state and the reactants. Its numerical value depends on standard-state conventions; association, molecular reorientation, internal motions and solvent reorganization can all contribute.
Activation enthalpy (ΔH‡∘)
Words: 32
Transition state theory OurBigBook.com
The standard enthalpy difference between the activated-complex reference state and the reactants at the same temperature and pressure. Under the usual Eyring assumptions it controls the slope of ln(k/T) against 1/T.
Eyring equation (k2​=hc∘kB​T​e−ΔG‡∘/RT)
Words: 26
Transition state theory OurBigBook.com
A transition state theory expression relating a rate constant to the standard free energy of activation. For a bimolecular reaction expressed in concentration units, k2​=(kB​T/h)(c∘)−1exp[−ΔG‡∘/(RT)] in the unit-transmission approximation.
Gibbs energy of activation (ΔG‡∘)
Words: 82 Articles: 2
Transition state theory OurBigBook.com
The Gibbs energy of activation is the standard molar Gibbs free energy change associated with going from the starting reactants to the transition state in transition state theory. It specifies the directional barrier, rather than the overall endpoint change in Gibbs free energy. Use consistent standard states when comparing Gibbs energies of activation and rate constants. See the IUPAC Gold Book: Gibbs energy of activation.
Enthalpy of activation (ΔH‡∘)
Words: 17
Gibbs energy of activation OurBigBook.com
The standard molar enthalpy difference between the transition state and the starting reactants, at the same temperature and pressure, in transition state theory.[ref]
Entropy of activation (ΔS‡∘)
Words: 20
Gibbs energy of activation OurBigBook.com
The standard molar entropy difference between the transition state and the starting reactants, at the same temperature and pressure, with specified standard states, in transition state theory.[ref]

Transition state

Words: 66
Chemical kinetics OurBigBook.com
A transition state describes configurations at the barrier between reactants and reaction products in an elementary reaction. It is a crossing region, rather than a stable substance that accumulates in a bottle. The IUPAC definition characterizes these configurations by equal probabilities of proceeding toward reactants or reaction products: [ref]. Lowering the barrier relative to the starting configuration can increase a reaction rate, even when the overall change in Gibbs free energy is unchanged.

Reaction rate (v)

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Chemical kinetics OurBigBook.com
For one chemical reaction in a closed system of fixed volume V, with uniform concentrations and no competing reactions or appreciable accumulation of unlisted species, choose the chemical equation
aA+bB⟶cC,a,b,c>0.
(36)
Brackets denote amount of substance per volume, for example [A]=nA​/V. The stoichiometry gives one instantaneous reaction rate
v=−a1​dtd[A]​=−b1​dtd[B]​=c1​dtd[C]​=V1​dtdξ​,
(37)
where ξ is the existing extent of reaction. The minus signs make forward consumption positive; dividing by the coefficients makes measurements of different chemical species agree. Units can be molL−1s−1. See IUPAC Gold Book: rate of reaction and Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §12.1: chemical reaction rates.
For the illustrative chemical equation 2A+B⟶3C, a measured d[C]/dt=0.060molL−1s−1 implies v=0.020molL−1s−1, d[A]/dt=−0.040molL−1s−1, and d[B]/dt=−0.020molL−1s−1. These numbers express stoichiometry, without supplying a rate law.
Each derivative is the slope of a concentration curve at one instant. Over a finite interval, −Δ[A]/(aΔt) instead gives an average reaction rate. For A converting reversibly to B, the net reaction rate is v=d[B]/dt=Jf​−Jr​; both directional reaction rates can remain positive when v=0 at chemical equilibrium.

Disappearance rate (vA​=−d[A]/dt)

Words: 58
Reaction rate OurBigBook.com
The disappearance rate of a reactant A is its positive net loss of concentration per unit time, vA​=−d[A]/dt. For the fixed-volume, single-chemical reaction setting of reaction rate, consuming a units of A per conversion gives vA​=av. The factor belongs to the stoichiometry; stating it is essential when quoting a rate constant. A negative net disappearance rate means that A is accumulating.

Rate law

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Reaction rate OurBigBook.com
A rate law specifies how a reaction rate depends on concentrations under stated conditions. A common form is
v=k[A]α[B]β,
(38)
where k is a rate constant and the exponents are partial orders of reaction. Determine them experimentally, or derive them from a justified reaction mechanism. Do not infer α=a and β=b from the net chemical equation: its coefficients describe consumption ratios, whereas the exponents describe sensitivity to concentration. See IUPAC Gold Book: rate law and Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §12.3: rate laws.
A rate law becomes a prediction of time evolution when combined with stoichiometry in a rate equation, for example d[A]/dt=−av. Agreement with a measured rate law is useful evidence for a reaction mechanism, but several routes can give the same dependence.

Integrated rate law

Words: 51
Rate law OurBigBook.com
An integrated rate law relates concentration to elapsed time after solving a rate equation with an initial condition. Its validity retains the assumptions of the underlying rate law, including fixed rate constants and appropriate stoichiometry. The second-order reaction reciprocal-concentration relation is one example; a different rate equation generally requires a different integrated rate law.[ref]

Order of reaction (n)

Words: 2k Articles: 7
Rate law OurBigBook.com
In a power-form rate law v=k[A]α[B]β, the partial orders of reaction are α and β, and the overall order of reaction is n=α+β. For example, doubling [A] at fixed [B] multiplies v by 2α: factors of one, two, and four correspond to partial orders of reaction zero, one, and two. These exponents can also be fractional or negative. A single constant order of reaction need not describe a rate law that is not a power form. See IUPAC Gold Book: order of reaction.
For a simple irreversible conversion A⟶B with rate equation −d[A]/dt=k[A]n, initial concentration A0​>0, and fixed k>0, compare zero-order reactions, first-order reactions, and second-order reactions using the dimensionless quantities
X=A0​[A]​,τ=kA0n−1​t,dτdX​=−Xn.
(39)
Their integrated curves, starting at X(0)=1, are
n=0:n=1:n=2:​X=1−τ(0≤τ<1),X=e−τ,X=1+τ1​.​
(40)
For the zero-order reaction, the plotted extension X=max(1−τ,0) stops conversion at depletion. It does not continue to obey dX/dτ=−1 once X=0. A negative concentration would be unphysical. The first-order reaction and second-order reaction approach zero without reaching it at finite time in these models.
The common τ axis compares curve shapes after each model's own time rescaling, rather than equal laboratory times for an identical numerical k. In the lower panels, X, lnX, and 1/X respectively give straight lines with slopes −1, −1, and +1 for the matching order of reaction. The natural logarithm uses a dimensionless quantity. These transformed plots help test a proposed rate law; the zero-order reaction line applies only before depletion. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §12.4: integrated rate laws.
First-order reaction
Words: 248 Articles: 1
Order of reaction OurBigBook.com
A first-order reaction has a reaction rate proportional to one reactant concentration in the simple single-species case. For an irreversible A⟶B in a closed system at fixed volume, take [A](0)=A0​, [B](0)=0, and constant rate constant k>0. Its rate equation and solution are
dtd[A]​=−k[A],[A](t)=A0​e−kt,[B](t)=A0​(1−e−kt),v(t)=kA0​e−kt.
(41)
A short check is enough: differentiating A0​e−kt gives −kA0​e−kt, and the two concentrations sum to A0​, as required by the one-to-one stoichiometry. Thus the same exponential decay describes both remaining reactant and decreasing reaction rate. Fixed k means a fixed fractional loss per unit time, not a fixed absolute consumption rate.
Choose illustrative values A0​=1molL−1 and k=0.2s−1, with t measured in seconds. Then [A]=e−0.2tmolL−1, [B]=(1−e−0.2t)molL−1, and v=0.2e−0.2tmolL−1s−1. The half-life is
t1/2​=kln2​=0.2ln2​s≈3.4657s.
(42)
At each successive half-life, half the remaining reactant is consumed; t1/2​ is independent of A0​ for this first-order reaction. At t=10s, the calculated values are [A]≈0.135335molL−1, [B]≈0.864665molL−1, and v≈0.027067molL−1s−1. These are model predictions for chosen parameters, rather than experimental measurements.
The left panel tracks the two concentrations; the right tracks their instantaneous conversion reaction rate. Their different vertical units matter: v=k[A], so the numerical curves need not have the same height. This gives a practical way to translate a measured concentration into a forecast of both conversion and waiting time.
First-order rate constant (k)
Words: 25
First-order reaction OurBigBook.com
The coefficient k of a first-order concentration term in a rate law. Its units are inverse time; two reversible first-order directions contribute additively to the relaxation rate.
Zero-order reaction
Words: 36
Order of reaction OurBigBook.com
A zero-order reaction has a reaction rate independent of the relevant reactant concentration over the range where its rate law applies. For A⟶B, [A]=A0​−kt is valid only before depletion at t=A0​/k. The constant-consumption model must stop or change there.
Second-order reaction
Words: 1k Articles: 2
Order of reaction OurBigBook.com
A second-order reaction has overall order of reaction two: a rate law may depend on [A]2, or on [A][B] with partial orders of reaction one and one. Doubling all relevant reactant concentrations multiplies the reaction rate by four at fixed conditions. This experimentally determined dependence does not establish molecularity or a unique reaction mechanism. For an elementary reaction obeying the law of mass action, molecularity and overall order of reaction agree; a net chemical equation alone cannot establish that the conversion is elementary.[ref]
For the single-concentration model, explicitly choose the disappearance rate convention
−dtd[A]​=kobs​[A]2,[A](0)=[A]0​>0,kobs​>0.
(43)
Here kobs​ is the coefficient for loss of A, held fixed at the specified temperature and other conditions. Its subscript labels the chosen observed disappearance rate; it does not imply a pseudo-first-order reaction. Assume a uniformly mixed closed system, fixed volume, and no appreciable reverse or competing chemical reactions. The integrated rate law is
[A](t)1​=[A]0​1​+kobs​t​,[A](t)=1+kobs​[A]0​t[A]0​​.
(44)
The reciprocal-concentration plot is a straight line with slope kobs​ and intercept 1/[A]0​. A brief derivation uses the chain rule: d(1/[A])/dt=−[A]−2d[A]/dt=kobs​, then applies the initial condition. This is a hyperbolic decay, rather than the exponential decay of a first-order reaction.[ref]
As an original prescribed example, choose [A]0​=0.020molL−1 and kobs​=0.50Lmol−1s−1. At t=100s, the reciprocal-concentration calculation is 50+50=100Lmol−1, giving [A]=0.010molL−1. The initial disappearance rate is 0.50(0.020)2=2.0×10−4molL−1s−1; after 100s it is 5.0×10−5molL−1s−1. Halving the concentration quarters the disappearance rate.
Dimensional analysis checks every formula: kobs​[A]2 has units molL−1s−1, kobs​t has units Lmol−1, and kobs​[A]0​t is a dimensionless quantity. Changing concentration units changes the numerical rate constant: the same example is [A]0​=20molm−3, kobs​=5.0×10−4m3mol−1s−1, giving [A](100s)=10molm−3.
For an elementary reaction 2A⟶P, instead define the stoichiometrically normalized reaction rate r=k[A]2. Two A entities disappear per P formed, so
r=−21​dtd[A]​=dtd[P]​=k[A]2,−dtd[A]​=2k[A]2,kobs​=2k.
(45)
Consequently the reciprocal-concentration slope is 2k, not k. In the prescribed example, the normalized rate constant would be k=0.25Lmol−1s−1; initially r=1.0×10−4molL−1s−1 while the disappearance rate is twice that. With [P](0)=0, stoichiometry gives [P](100s)=([A]0​−[A])/2=0.0050molL−1. Both rate constants have the same dimensions, so a units check alone cannot catch their factor-of-two difference. The symbol r denotes the same normalization as v in reaction rate.
The half-life, meaning the time to reach half a specified starting concentration, follows by setting [A]=[A]0​/2:
t1/2​=kobs​[A]0​1​​.
(46)
For r=k[A]2 in 2A⟶P, this becomes t1/2​=1/(2k[A]0​). Its units are seconds because kobs​[A]0​ has units s−1. Doubling the starting concentration halves the first half-life; a quoted half-life needs its starting concentration. This differs from a first-order reaction, whose half-life is independent of starting concentration.[ref]
Within the prescribed run, [A] reaches 0.010, 0.0050, and 0.0025molL−1 at 100, 300, and 700s. The successive halving intervals are 100, 200, and 400s: each begins at a smaller concentration. More generally, reaching fraction f of the initial concentration, with 0<f<1, requires t=(f−1−1)/(kobs​[A]0​), so 90% consumption takes nine initial half-lives, rather than a fixed sequence of equal waiting times.
A straight reciprocal-concentration plot tests this particular single-concentration rate equation. It does not uniquely identify a reaction mechanism, nor does curvature rule out every second-order reaction: two independently changing reactant concentrations require their own integrated rate law. At low concentration, a small measurement error δ[A] becomes approximately −δ[A]/[A]2 in the reciprocal, magnifying late-time errors. Use the line as a diagnostic; a nonlinear regression of the original concentrations can retain their measurement scale and explicit error model.
Unequal-concentration second-order integration (ln(hx0​/(xh0​))=kΔt)
Words: 25
Second-order reaction OurBigBook.com
For a one-to-one elementary reaction with concentrations x and h, the difference Δ=h0​−x0​ remains constant. Integration gives ln(hx0​/(xh0​))=kΔt when Δ=0; the equal-initial-concentration limit is 1/x−1/x0​=kt.
Conductometric saponification assay
Words: 502
Second-order reaction OurBigBook.com
How can an invisible change in concentration produce a readable signal? The saponification of ethyl acetate by hydroxide in water gives ethanol and an acetate ion:
CH3​COOC2​H5​+OH−⟶CH3​COO−+C2​H5​OH.
(47)
The rate law used for this assay is r=k2​[ethyl acetate][OH−]. Each reactant has coefficient one, so r equals either disappearance rate. If the two initial concentrations are equal, they remain equal under this stoichiometry, giving −dc/dt=k2​c2 and kobs​=k2​, without a factor of two.
Manual for Advanced Physical Chemistry Laboratory-II by Nasima Arshad (Unit 7, Experiment 2, printed pp. 66–67) specifies a conductivity cell holding about 60mL in constant-temperature baths, with 0.040molL−1 ethyl acetate and sodium hydroxide stocks equilibrated separately. Mixing 30mL of each initiates the run. The readout is electrical resistance: every minute for ten minutes, every two minutes for ten more, then every five minutes for twenty-five. The cell is rinsed with distilled water. A matched sodium hydroxide–water dilution estimates the initial resistance; a potassium chloride standard determines the cell constant. The manual asks for comparison with the extrapolated initial signal.[ref]
The post-mixing initial concentration is c0​=0.040(30/60)=0.020molL−1 for each reactant, assuming additive volumes. This matches our illustrative starting concentration, but the prescribed kobs​=0.50 is not a measured value from the manual. As hydroxide is replaced by the less mobile acetate ion, electrical conductance decreases. The preceding experiment describes two platinum electrodes and an alternating-voltage Wheatstone bridge to limit polarization at the electrodes. For measured electrical resistance R(t), electrical conductance is G(t)=1/R(t); electrical conductivity is κ(t)=Kcell​G(t). Keep the probe geometry fixed and use one signal convention throughout.[ref]
For the equal-starting-concentration model, assume an affine calibration between electrical conductance and remaining hydroxide concentration, with endpoints G0​ and G∞​ at the same temperature. This gives
c0​c(t)​=G0​−G∞​G(t)−G∞​​,G(t)−G∞​G0​−G(t)​=c(t)c0​−c(t)​=k2​c0​t.
(48)
The last plot has slope k2​c0​, with units s−1, whereas plotting 1/c against time has slope k2​, with units Lmol−1s−1. These are different slopes. This endpoint transformation also shows why raw resistance must not be substituted for conductance.
Useful additional controls are repeat runs, fixed immersion depth, an independently checked final signal, and comparisons of several starting concentrations. Mixing delay obscures early conversion; temperature drift changes both the rate constant and the signal; contamination adds mobile ions. The affine calibration can fail when ionic mobilities change with composition. Near completion, G−G∞​ becomes small, so endpoint error is strongly amplified. Those are methodological limits and proposed checks, not new experimental observations. A conductivity trace supports a calibrated rate law over its tested range; it does not independently reveal the full reaction mechanism.
For unequal starting concentrations a=[A]0​ and b=[B]0​ in a one-to-one chemical reaction, let x be the consumed concentration. Then [A]=a−x, [B]=b−x, and
dtdx​=k2​(a−x)(b−x),b−a1​ln(b(a−x)a(b−x)​)=k2​t(a=b).
(49)
The natural logarithm acts on a dimensionless quantity; differentiating the left side with respect to x gives 1/((a−x)(b−x)), verifying the relation. Mixing 20mL of the stated ethyl acetate stock with 40mL of the sodium hydroxide stock would give a=0.01333… and b=0.02666…molL−1. The difference [B]−[A]=b−a stays constant, rather than their ratio. Neither the equal-concentration reciprocal formula nor a pseudo-first-order reaction approximation is justified solely by that twofold excess.
Pseudo-first-order reaction
Words: 123
Order of reaction OurBigBook.com
In a second-order reaction A+B⟶P with rate law −d[A]/dt=k2​[A][B], a large excess of B can keep [B]≈[B]0​ during the observation window. Then
−dtd[A]​≈k1​[A],k1​=k2​[B]0​,[A](t)≈[A]0​e−k1​t.
(50)
This is a pseudo-first-order reaction: the approximate first-order reaction describes that window, while changing the excess B concentration changes k1​. Its units are s−1, distinct from the second-order reaction rate constant k2​. For one-to-one stoichiometry, the maximum fractional depletion of B is [A]0​/[B]0​; an original 100:1 initial excess bounds its change by 1%. A twofold excess permits 50% depletion and does not provide the same control.[ref]

Rate constant (k)

Words: 114
Chemical kinetics OurBigBook.com
A rate constant is the coefficient in a specified rate law, held fixed under specified conditions. It can describe an empirical overall chemical reaction, as well as an elementary reaction. Fixed temperature matters: changing temperature can change k, even for the same chemical reaction. See IUPAC Gold Book: order of reaction and rate constants and IUPAC Gold Book: rate coefficient.
For v=k[A]n, dimensional consistency requires
units(k)=(molL−1)1−ns−1.
(51)
A zero-order reaction therefore uses molL−1s−1; a first-order reaction uses s−1; a second-order reaction uses Lmol−1s−1. Comparing bare numerical values of k across different orders of reaction is meaningless without their units and concentrations. Even for the same order of reaction, state whether k multiplies the normalized reaction rate v or a particular reactant disappearance rate: a stoichiometric coefficient can change that convention.
